variants.name: Package-private implementation with a public narrow attorney class
variants.idiom_name: package-private implementation plus a public narrow attorney class in the same package (Java 1+); a module qualified export when the grant crosses a module boundary (Java 9+)
variants.implementation_notes: Java has no per-collaborator grant; what it has is package access - a member or top-level class declared without a modifier is accessible throughout its package and nowhere else (JLS 6.6.1) - plus nested classes that can reach the enclosing class's private members, plus the module system's qualified export, which hands one package to exactly one named module (JEP 261). The idiomatic realization is therefore: keep the implementation class package-private, give the attorney a public class in the same package whose methods are the only granted calls, and have the attorney own the private implementation so callers never name it. The hand-built attorney is still justified when a single type in another package must be the only caller - Java cannot say that - so a module boundary plus the attorney's narrow surface is the accepted approximation.
pitfalls: Package access is package-granular: every class in the same package can call Grid.recalc, so the narrow surface is held by convention and review, not by javac.

Do not name the implementation type in the attorney's public signature (no public Grid field, parameter or return value): once callers can hold the type they can call its whole package-private surface, and the grant has silently widened.
Reflection (setAccessible) and, on the class path, plain visibility reach package-private members at run time; treat the boundary as compile-time organisation, not as a security control.

variants.name: JPMS qualified export: the module system grants one package to one named module
variants.implementation_notes: The module system is the only Java mechanism that grants access to a named collaborator rather than to a whole scope: 'exports com.example.grid.internal to com.example.helper' makes the package readable by exactly that module while every other module - and the unnamed module of the class path - sees nothing (JEP 261 calls this a qualified export; the accessibility rules are JLS 6.6.1). Use it when the grant crosses a module boundary, and combine it with a narrow attorney class inside the exported package when the granted surface must be narrow as well, because the qualified export itself is package- and module-granular, not type-granular.
pitfalls: 'to' names modules, not types: every class in the target module gains access to the whole package, and that module can re-expose what it sees through its own public API.
The class path, --add-exports/--add-opens and modular reflection can override the boundary at compile or run time, so a qualified export is a build-time contract rather than enforced isolation.
